🚀 Byte Busters looking for teammates!
I'm handling backend—need frontend devs, designers, or anyone down to brainstorm and build.
summary:
We built an offline-first web dashboard that monitors astronaut health during long missions and, unlike most health trackers, monitors the medicines the crew takes. It tracks sleep, heart rate, stress, mood and exercise against each astronaut’s own 14-day baseline, so an alert means “this is unusual for this person,” not just “outside a fixed range.” A medication layer logs doses, warns about interactions, asks follow-up questions after each dose to check whether the drug worked, and flags stored medicines whose potency may be at risk. It runs on simulated data.

The challenge asks for software that tracks astronauts’ physical and psychological stress. Our app does this through a crew overview, per-astronaut trend charts, and prioritized alerts that each give a one-line reason. It works offline, which matters because Moon and Mars communication will be delayed.

On deep-space missions, crews must catch problems early and rely on the medicines they carry. NASA research shows astronauts sleep about six hours against eight recommended, that sleep drugs shorten time to fall asleep without clearly increasing total sleep, and that stored drugs can degrade faster in flight. Our app turns these findings into personalized early warning, drug effectiveness checks, and stored-medicine risk flags.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Picture a quiet medical officer who never sleeps, travels with the crew, and needs no Earth connection. Each day it learns what “normal” looks like for every astronaut, in sleep, heart rate, stress, mood and exercise. When someone starts to drift from their own normal, it raises a green, yellow or red status with a one-line reason, and it projects the trend 48 hours ahead so the flight surgeon sees trouble coming. It also suggests possible causes, such as fluid shift, fatigue or drug tolerance, as ideas to check, never as a diagnosis.

Alongside the crew, it watches the medicine cabinet. It logs doses, warns about combinations NASA’s kit checklist advises against, asks quick “did it help?” questions after each dose, and gives every stored medicine a green, yellow or red potency risk flag.

What benefits does it have?

  • It catches slow decline that fixed limits miss, because each person is compared with themselves.
  • Every alert explains itself, so the clinician can trust it.
  • It shows whether a drug actually helps, not just whether it was taken.
  • It tells the crew which stored medicines to rely on when resupply is impossible.
  • It runs offline, with no data leaving the device.

What is the intended impact?

We want future Moon and Mars crews to get earlier warning and use their limited medicine supply more safely. The same approach could help remote clinics and expedition teams on Earth, where doctors are far away too.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

TypeScript, React and Vite for the offline web app. The learning models are written from scratch, with no outside machine-learning libraries and no cloud: a personal baseline that updates daily, Bayesian updating for drug effectiveness, and a simple trend projection. A synthetic data generator creates a 30-day crew with problems built in so alerts can be demonstrated. No special hardware is needed. We grounded the work in NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, NASA’s sleep evidence report and brief, the ISS medical kit checklist, and the 2023 study of flown drugs by Reichard and colleagues.

How is it creative?

Most space health projects stop at vitals. We asked a question few ask: “the astronaut is struggling, but is the medicine helping, and is it still any good?” We combine a pharmacist’s view with a self-learning early-warning engine and turn NASA’s own research findings into working features.

What factors did your team consider?

Communication delay, which means it must run offline. Trust, so every alert gives a reason and supports the clinician without replacing them. Spacecraft conditions, so the interface is low-glare and colours are always paired with words. Evidence, so we used NASA sources wherever we found them. Honesty, since all data is simulated, some clinical ranges are placeholders, and the potency flag is a risk indicator, not a measured value.
dataRefs: NASA ISS Medical Kit Contents and Reference (drug list, side effects, interaction warnings)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief: Pharmaceutical Care (spaceflight effects on drug uptake and stability)
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief: Sleep Accommodations (in-flight sleep duration and sleep medicine findings)
NASA Human Research Program Evidence Report: Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload
